name: Carlos Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. First, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Carlos, 27, and I work at Hollins Farm, which is a big pig unit with about 400 acres of maize and wheat around it. There are eight of us on the staff and I'm the newest, two years in. My partner Amira is a nurse on the night shift at the district hospital, and we're saving for a house. We've got about ten months of money put away, which sounds like a lot until you look at house prices.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at six in the farrowing house, checking the sows and the new litters, then I help Dev, the head stockman, with weaning and moving pigs between sheds. The feeding's already mostly automatic in the finishing sheds, so a lot of my job is watching screens and then walking the pens to check the screens are right. In autumn I'm on the maize harvest, driving the trailer behind the forage harvester. I like the piglets and the harvest rush. What wears me out is the smell in your hair and the hours in September.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the tools are handy but they're not magic. Amira and I already use a chatbot now and then for writing emails to the landlord. I'd post something like, still need someone to pick up the piglet that got stuck behind the heat lamp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's fine for me. My worry was never chatbots, it was robots in the sheds. If it plateaus, the real question goes back to what it's always been, which is whether the big buyers squeeze the farm on price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, mainly. I'd ask Dev to let me do more of the sow health checks, because that's how you move up. And we'd keep saving for the deposit at the same rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the boring version, and boring is good when you're trying to buy a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the feeding is already automatic. Does that make you more or less confident in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More confident. The automatic feeders came in four years ago and they still need a person to walk the pens every day. They break, they block, a pig gets sick and the screen doesn't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens with the house plans if nothing much changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same plan. Another year and a half of saving, then we buy something small in town, near the hospital for Amira. That's been the plan since we moved in together.

S0.say: I'd say the tools are handy but not magic. I'd post that you still need someone to pick up the piglet stuck behind the heat lamp.
S0.think: Privately he's fine with it, because his worry was always robots in the sheds rather than chatbots. The real pressure goes back to big buyers squeezing the farm on price.
S0.do: Keeps going and asks the head stockman for more sow health checks to move up. Keeps saving for a house deposit at the same rate.
S0.feel: Calm. The boring version suits someone trying to buy a house.
S0.quote: They break, they block, a pig gets sick and the screen doesn't know.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos already works alongside automatic feeders, so he has a grounded view of what machines can and can't do in a pig unit. His concern about buyers squeezing prices shows his politics quietly. The house is the centre of his plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to happen, so let's make sure workers get a fair share of what the farms save. I'd bring it up at the union, because most farmworkers aren't even in one. Online I'd probably share a petition or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it shrinks the staff at Hollins from eight to five or six. I'm the newest, so I'd be nervous. But I also think the people who learn the machines first keep their jobs, and I can learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to go on the training when the farm brings in the next machines, whatever they are, and I'd use the AI tools more to understand them. I'd join the farmworkers' union properly and get a couple of the others to join too. We'd keep saving, maybe a bit slower on the house while we watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. I think I'd be all right, but I'd be watching Dev's face every time a sales rep came round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Hollins would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shirley, who's been in the sheds 30 years and won't touch a tablet. She knows more about pigs than anyone I've met. If the farm only keeps people who can work the screens, she's out, and that's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use chatbots now and then. Would that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, probably. Once Dev or the vet started using it to check pig health records, I'd use it too. I'm not the first one in, but I don't like being the last one either.

S1.say: He'd say it's going to happen, so workers should get a fair share of what farms save. He'd raise it at the union and share a petition or two.
S1.think: Privately he thinks the staff at Hollins shrinks from eight to five or six, and as the newest he'd be nervous. He believes the people who learn the machines first keep their jobs.
S1.do: Asks to go on the training when the farm brings in new machines and uses AI tools more to understand them. Joins the farmworkers' union properly and recruits a couple of colleagues.
S1.feel: Uneasy. He thinks he'd be all right but would be watching every sales visit.
S1.quote: If the farm only keeps people who can work the screens, she's out, and that's wrong.
S1.fieldNote: His steady streak shows clearly: he'd learn the tools, but only once the vet or head stockman did. His worry for Shirley, the older stockwoman, is where his politics become personal. He frames fairness as sharing the savings with workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to step in now, with a basic income or wage support, because nobody's ready. I'd be at the union meetings and probably at a march. I'd say farmworkers and nurses should stand together on this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd think my job's gone within a year of it arriving. A robot that can farrow sows and drive the trailer doesn't need me. I'm not panicking, because we've got savings and Amira's job, but I'm not kidding myself either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the house hunt straight away and keep the deposit as a cushion. I'd sign up for whatever union campaign there was, push for wage support, and look at jobs nearby that might last a bit longer, maybe repairing the machines. Then we'd sit tight and see where the dust settles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like standing in the farrowing house when the power goes and you don't know when it's coming back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What happens to the house in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It goes on hold. Buying a house with a mortgage when neither of us knows if we'll have a wage in 2029 would be mad. The deposit becomes our emergency money, which hurts, because we worked for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Amira's job is hands-on too. How do you two talk about this at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk at the kitchen table at two in the afternoon, when she's just up and I'm on my break. She'd say hospitals will always need people, and I'd say that's what the farm said about pigs. Then we'd laugh, because what else do you do.

S2.say: He'd say the government needs to step in now with a basic income or wage support, because nobody's ready. He'd say farmworkers and nurses should stand together.
S2.think: Privately he thinks his job's gone within a year of arrival. He's not panicking because of savings and his partner's income, but he isn't kidding himself either.
S2.do: Stops the house hunt at once and keeps the deposit as an emergency cushion. Joins the union campaign for wage support and looks at machine repair work nearby.
S2.feel: Anxious, like waiting in the dark after a power cut with no idea when it'll come back.
S2.quote: She'd say hospitals will always need people, and I'd say that's what the farm said about pigs.
S2.fieldNote: His cushion and his partner's job keep him out of panic, and he says so himself. The house is the first casualty, and turning the deposit into emergency money clearly stings. He reaches for public support and solidarity across jobs, which fits his outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan properly, so the government has no excuse. I'd want them funding retraining for rural workers now, not when it hits. I'd say it at the union and on the local farming group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is just about enough for me to become the person who fixes the robots instead of the person they replace. That's not forever, but it's something. I'd be 32, and still young enough to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start an evening course in agricultural engineering at the college, the kind with hydraulics and electrics. I'd ask Hollins to let me shadow the engineer when he services the feeders. We'd hold off on the house for a year or two and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's a working kind of uneasy. I'd have something to do with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with the two-year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get a qualification, mainly. With two years I'd just be protecting money. With five I can actually change what I do, and the money is there to cover the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first about a plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev first, because he knows what's coming before anyone. Then Amira, obviously. And probably the union rep, to ask if they'd pay for the course.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to plan properly, so the government has no excuse. He'd want funding for rural retraining now, not later.
S3.think: Privately he thinks five years is just about enough to become the person who fixes the robots instead of the one they replace. At 32 he'd still be young enough to switch.
S3.do: Starts an evening agricultural engineering course at the college in the first year. Shadows the farm engineer when he services the feeders, and puts the house on hold for a year or two.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but in a working way, with something to do about it.
S3.quote: Five years is just about enough for me to become the person who fixes the robots instead of the person they replace.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time changes his stance from defending money to building a new skill. He has a concrete, realistic path through engineering. He still wants public money for retraining, but here he's willing to pay for it himself if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it. Everyone should get proper training, and farms that bring in robots should keep paying into a fund for the people they let go. I'd say that at the union and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it feels manageable for me. I'm 27, I've got savings, and I'll learn things once I see they work. The danger is that I get comfortable and wait too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd buy the house, probably next year as planned, because ten years of a mortgage paid down is worth something. I'd start the engineering course within two years, once I see which machines are actually turning up. And I'd keep putting money aside every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more about the world than about me. I'd be thinking about Shirley again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still put the house on hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd buy it. If it's ten years out, a house is the one thing that's still worth something when it arrives. And Amira wants a garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running the machines for a few farms, maybe, or fixing them. Something where I'm still out in the yard. I don't want to sit in an office, even if the office is a phone.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it. Farms that bring in robots should pay into a fund for the people they let go.
S4.think: Privately he thinks it's manageable: he's young, has savings and learns things once he sees they work. His main fear is getting comfortable and waiting too long.
S4.do: Buys the house next year as planned and starts the engineering course within two years. Keeps putting money aside every month.
S4.feel: Uneasy, more for the world and for older colleagues than for himself.
S4.quote: If it's ten years out, a house is the one thing that's still worth something when it arrives. And Amira wants a garden.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, the house goes back on, and he sees it as the one safe asset. His steady habit of waiting for proof is something he recognises as a risk. His worry shifts back to Shirley, which shows his politics are tied to real people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it wrecks the house and there's no time to learn anything. What would help is wage support straight away, from the government, and courses that are free and in the evening so people can still work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the older ones, like Shirley. People my age will find something. The ones with 30 years in a pig shed are the ones who'll get forgotten, and they're the ones who taught me everything.

headlineQuote: The ones with 30 years in a pig shed are the ones who'll get forgotten, and they're the ones who taught me everything.
portrait: Carlos Dubois is a 27-year-old junior stockman at Hollins Farm, a large pig unit with maize and wheat, where he already works alongside automatic feeders. He lives with his partner Amira, a night-shift nurse, and they've saved about ten months of money for a house deposit. He's progressive, a union member and a steady adopter who learns new tools once the vet or head stockman does. The two-year AGI picture freezes the house and makes him anxious, while five and ten years give him time for an engineering course and a plan to fix the robots instead of being replaced by them.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it wrecks the house plans and leaves no time to learn anything.
whatWouldHelp: Immediate wage support from the government, and free evening courses so people can keep working while they retrain.
